records.name_note: Sources split on which form of the common name is primary. NC State's Common Name(s) field is a stacked, alphabetized list (Common Golden Alexander, Golden Alexanders, Meadow Parsnip, Wild Parsley) that marks no entry as primary -- its own body prose is what actually names the plant, and it uses 'Golden Alexanders' (plural). RHS leads with the plural too: its H1 is the bare botanical name with 'golden alexanders' as the plant-profile subtitle (and in the page title), and 'wild parsley' sits separately under 'Other common names'. Two admissible sources lead with the singular: MoBot's displayed 'Common Name:' field reads 'golden Alexander' (a Common Names popup behind it adds 'meadow parsnip' and 'wild parsley'), and Penn State Extension's dedicated page is titled 'Rain Garden Plants: Golden Alexander (Zizia aurea)'. The cited sources therefore split two plural to two singular; the plural 'Golden Alexanders' was chosen because it is the form NC State's own running prose and RHS's profile use. Separately, NC State is the only admissible source carrying a structured 'is often confused with' module, and it names Sanicula canadensis rather than Wild Parsnip (Pastinaca sativa); MoBot's confusable remark is body prose and names Zizia aptera. So the well-documented Zizia/Pastinaca look-alike relationship could not be sourced from an admissible structured module.
unknowns: No admissible source (NC State, MoBot, RHS, Clemson HGIC, PSU Extension) carries any toxicity, poison, or pet-safety information for Zizia aurea specifically — NC State's page, which does carry a structured Poison block and Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags on many species, has none for this one. toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are left null rather than inferred from the Apiaceae family in general.

is_houseplant is left null: every admissible source describes this species only as an outdoor native perennial for gardens, prairies, woodland edges, or rain gardens (NC State, MoBot, RHS, Clemson, PSU); none explicitly states it is or is not grown as a houseplant.

Indoor/greenhouse climate fields (day_f/night_f min-max, humidity_need/pct, light_fc_min/good) are left null — no admissible source gives indoor temperature, humidity, or footcandle figures for this outdoor perennial; sources instead give USDA hardiness zones (NC State 3a-8b; MoBot Zone 3-8; RHS H5), which are survival ratings, not climate-control targets.
chill_damage_f is left null: the only cold-tolerance data found are hardiness-zone ratings, which rule 9 excludes as a proxy for a damage-onset temperature; no source states a literal onset figure.

soil_ph_min/max are left null: NC State's page for this species has no Soil pH field at all, and RHS's pH field lists Acid, Alkaline, and Neutral all as acceptable, so per the rules no ceiling (blocked by RHS allowing alkaline) or floor (blocked by RHS allowing acid) can be set.

water_regime is left null: no admissible source frames watering for this species as an imperative regime (keep moist vs. dry between). MoBot's structured field reads 'Water: Medium', which is mid-scale and, per the rules, cannot itself support keep_moist; it is noted here only as a disclosed counterpoint, not used to set the field.

PSU Extension's rain-garden page for this species gives 'Soil: Moist, sandy, sandy-clay soils' and 'Hydrologic Zones: Wet/moist' — per the rules these describe stormwater-basin siting suitability, not a cultivation drainage statement, so they were not used to override the moderate soil_drainage reading drawn from NC State's and RHS's species cultivation fields, and were not used to set water_regime either.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis, and the fertilize_* fields are all left null: this is an in-ground garden/prairie perennial and no admissible source frames watering on a dry-down or day-interval basis, nor discusses fertilizing it at all.

direct_sun_hours_max is left null: NC State's Light field text ('Full sun (6 or more hours...)', 'Partial Shade (2-6 hours)') matches that site's generic, site-wide light-category legend definitions rather than species-specific prose about this plant's own sun tolerance, so per the rules it was not used.
light_fc_min/good could not be sourced from any admissible domain for this species.

RHS leads with 'wild senna' -- it is the sole entry in Other common names and the only common name on the profile, appearing as the page subtitle and in the page title 'Senna hebecarpa | wild senna'. 'Wild Senna' is used here as common_name because RHS names a single common name for the species with no alternative offered, with 'American Senna' recorded as NC State's own preferred usage.
unknowns: No admissible source (NC State, RHS, or the others searched) provides a toxicity assessment scoped to cats and/or dogs for Senna hebecarpa. NC State's page for this species has no Poison/toxicity section at all (unlike some other NC State plant pages), and RHS's static page content carries no toxicity field either. Non-admissible sources (picturethisai.com, plantids.com, localeaf.ca, plantiary.com) do describe GI-upset risk to cats and dogs from senna's anthraquinone compounds, but per the admissible-domain restriction these cannot be used, so toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are left null rather than inferred from genus-level anthraquinone chemistry or non-admissible sources.

RHS's static page for Senna hebecarpa (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/69841/senna-hebecarpa/details) carries no rendered Hardiness, Soil, pH, Moisture, Aspect/Sun Exposure, or Position fields at all (confirmed by inspecting the raw page source) -- only Family, Genus description, Native to GB/Ireland, Name Status, and common-name/synonym fields are present. Because RHS provides no pH field to cross-check NC State's closed 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' band in either direction as required, soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are left null rather than reading a ceiling/floor off NC State's band alone.

water_regime is left null: the only structured moisture data found is University of Maryland Extension's Coastal Plain meadow-species table, which checks Moist, Average, AND Dry as suitable moisture conditions (with Wet and Extra Dry unchecked) for Senna hebecarpa -- a three-way tolerance span rather than a single watering statement or regime, so no single enum value is clearly supported. NC State's page has no dedicated Water Requirements field or watering-statement prose for this species.

records.name_note: Four admissible sources bear on the common name and three of them assert a lead: MoBot leads with false aster, RHS's plant-profile subtitle leads with false chamomile, and UMD's caption leads with Eastern Doll's Daisy; NC State asserts no lead at all, giving only an alphabetized five-name list. Each page is structured differently. NC State's Common Name(s) field is an alphabetized, stacked list of five names -- Boltonia, Eastern Doll's Daisy, False Aster, False Chamomile, White Doll's Daisy -- with no entry marked as primary (the first entry, "Boltonia," is an alphabetization artifact, not a lead name); NC State's own body-description prose instead opens with "False chamomile is a perennial in the daisy family...", making False Chamomile the name the article's running text actually uses. Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder species page (taxonid 277173 -- the species page, distinct from the var. latisquama and 'Snowbank' cultivar pages) shows an affirmative, single "Common Name: false aster" field, with a longer "Common Names" tooltip/popup behind it listing false aster, bolton's starwort, false chamomile, and flase starwort [MoBot's own misspelling] in that order; however MoBot's own Noteworthy Characteristics prose calls the plant "commonly called false chamomile or false aster," putting chamomile first. RHS's dedicated species-level plant profile (plant ID 72681; the H1 is the botanical name alone) carries "false chamomile" as both its plant-profile subtitle and page title, and no "Other common names" field appears on that page. University of Maryland Extension captions the species "Boltonia asteroides (Eastern Doll's Daisy)". MoBot is the only source that labels the assertion -- an explicit single-value "Common Name:" field -- whereas RHS's competing single name appears only as an unlabeled subtitle; this record follows MoBot's labeled designation, False Aster, while flagging that RHS's subtitle, NC State's running prose, and UMD's caption all lead elsewhere.

chill_damage_f left null: no admissible source states a numeric cold-damage-onset temperature; NC State and MoBot instead give a USDA hardiness range (zones 3-10), which is a survival/growing-range rating, not an onset figure, per the rules for this field.
